summary: This memo is a reprint of a RARE technical report that compares the proposals for the next version of IP, then under discussion because the existing addressing system was running out of room. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet was running out of addresses, so several groups proposed fixes. This paper compares their ideas side by side.

questions: comparison of next version of ip proposals
ipv6 candidate proposals pip sip tuba
why did ipv4 run out of addresses
subtitle: Comparing three candidate designs for the next version of the Internet Protocol.

tldr.problem: By the early 1990s, IPv4 was running out of address space due to exponential Internet growth. Three main proposals emerged to replace IPv4: PIP, SIP, and TUBA. Each took different approaches to solving address exhaustion and other limitations, but all faced similar technical and practical challenges.
tldr.mechanism: The three proposals all provided larger address spaces and supported routing aggregation, source routing, multicast, and encapsulation. The main differences were in header design (PIP with opaque fields), minimalism (SIP with reduced features), and reuse of ISO standards (TUBA). Each included transition mechanisms to coexist with IPv4.
tldr.outcome: The RFC was published during the selection process; eventually IPv6 (Stagewise Hexadecimal Internet Protocol) was chosen, though not one of these three exact proposals. However, the analysis remains relevant as a snapshot of the architectural thinking in 1993.

today: RFC 1454 documents the proposals being evaluated in 1993. IPv6, eventually standardized, drew from all three proposals but was not identical to any. The RFC remains valuable as a snapshot of architectural thinking during the transition, showing how the community weighed design trade-offs between flexibility, simplicity, and reuse. Many issues deferred in 1993 (security, autoconfiguration, mobile hosts) became topics of subsequent RFCs and standards.

sections.title: Why IPv4 Was Becoming Inadequate
sections.content:
By the early 1990s, IPv4's 32-bit address space faced exhaustion. The immediate problem was depletion of Class B address blocks—a middle tier of addresses commonly assigned to organizations. More fundamentally, the flat routing space created by non-hierarchical address allocation was preventing route aggregation, causing routing tables to grow explosively.

The Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) recognized that simple extensions to IPv4 would not suffice. Interim remedies like CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) and improved routing protocols like OSPF and BGP could buy time, but a longer-term solution required a new protocol. The community had until the 26th IETF meeting in March 1993 to select among candidates, each with interoperable implementations and transition plans.
sections.plainLanguage: The old Internet was using 32-bit addresses (about 4 billion possible addresses), but there were already so many computers that we were running out. You could not just make IPv4 bigger—the whole design needed to change.

sections.title: Common Features of All Proposals
sections.content:
All three proposals shared fundamental characteristics. Each provided larger addresses to enable hierarchical allocation and route aggregation. All assumed a routing implementation philosophy, focusing on the internals of routing within networks rather than on the end-user service. All three treated the new protocol as universal—the same network-layer protocol would handle links, hosts, and router-to-router communication. This was a conservative choice, driven by time pressure and risk aversion.

All proposals supported source routing (allowing sources to specify paths through the network) and encapsulation (nesting one packet inside another to redirect it). Multicast addressing, fragmentation, and hop-count limits were supported across all three. However, all three reconfigured IPv4's "Time to Live" field as a simple hop-count, raising unresolved questions about the maximum lifetime of packets in the network—a constraint needed by transport-layer protocols to ensure sequence numbers and fragment IDs never collide.
sections.plainLanguage: All three candidates made addresses much bigger, supported routing tricks like source routing, and let packets be wrapped inside other packets. They all kept the same basic philosophy as IPv4: simple, universal, incremental.

sections.title: The Three Proposals: PIP, SIP, and TUBA
sections.content:
PIP (P Internet Protocol) offered the most flexibility and innovation. Its header contained instructions to routers' forwarding processors, effectively allowing sources to write small routing programs. PIP addresses had effectively unlimited length, scaling hierarchically with network topology. However, this flexibility came at a cost: PIP defined opaque fields whose meaning could vary between administrative domains, requiring border routers to negotiate and translate encodings—a significant implementation burden.

SIP (Simple IP) took the minimalist approach: it was IP with larger addresses (64 bits) and fewer options. Its main advantage was processing efficiency—even simpler than IPv4. Its main disadvantage was fundamental: it was unclear whether 64 bits would be adequate for the foreseeable future, and extension for new features was not obvious.

TUBA (TCP/UDP with Big Addresses) reused the ISO CLNP (Connectionless Network Protocol) standard with its 20-byte addresses and ES-IS router discovery mechanism. This leveraged existing router implementations but faced criticism: it offered little more than larger addresses, and the control protocol had efficiency issues on large LANs. However, TUBA's router-discovery mechanism provided a path to automatic host configuration, absent from the other proposals.
sections.plainLanguage: PIP was fancy—sources could tell routers how to route packets. SIP was simple—just bigger addresses, nothing else. TUBA reused an existing standard from the ISO world. Each had trade-offs: flexibility, simplicity, or reuse.

sections.title: Unresolved Issues Across All Proposals
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several critical issues none of the proposals adequately addressed. Resource reservation was hinted at but unspecified—applications needed ways to reserve bandwidth and declare requirements, but no mechanisms were defined. Address assignment policies remained unclear; the larger space invited new choices (geographic versus provider-based allocation), but consequences for address lifetime and DNS were not fully worked out.

Automatic configuration was recognized as essential (manual IP configuration was notoriously difficult) but remained for future work. Proposals mentioned some possibilities—deriving addresses from LAN addresses, dynamic assignment, generic well-known addresses for local services—but did not commit to solutions. Application interface and protocol changes were necessary because many applications (FTP, RPC) hardcoded IPv4 address handling, but transition mechanisms were sketched rather than fully specified. DNS changes needed to support larger addresses, but detailed design was incomplete. Additionally, congestion avoidance, mobile host support, accounting, and security received little attention—often deferred to "for further study."
sections.plainLanguage: The three proposals solved the address problem but left a lot of other stuff for later: How do you ask the network to reserve bandwidth? How do you automatically set up a new computer? What happens when you move to a different Internet provider? How do we keep bad guys from spoofing addresses?

sections.title: Transition Mechanisms and Coexistence
sections.content:
A crucial aspect of any new protocol is the ability to coexist with the old one during transition. All proposals required either that new hosts also support IPv4, or that translators convert between protocols. Additionally, the network infrastructure needed to carry both protocols, or tunneling/translation mechanisms had to encapsulate one protocol within another. The proposals offered different combinations of these approaches.

One thorny problem was tunneling across IPv4 networks: extra address information from the larger address space had to be carried somehow, either as new headers or as IPv4 options. New IPv4 options risked being discarded by routers that did not recognize them. Longer headers in tunneling made error reporting complex. Some feared a "new version of IPv4" might be needed just to support tunneling. Alternatively, new hosts could maintain dual stacks (both protocols), but this required mechanisms to choose which protocol to use.
sections.plainLanguage: You cannot flip a switch and upgrade the whole Internet overnight. Old computers will keep using IPv4 while new ones use the new protocol. The tricky part is getting them to talk to each other during the transition.

sections.title: Reflections on Process and Convergence
sections.content:
The RFC notes that this was the first fundamental change to Internet protocols since the Internet was manageable and development tied to US government contracts. The IETF/IESG/IAB structures had not evolved to manage change of this magnitude. Interestingly, many perceived problems of the OSI standardization process—slow progress, factional infighting, convergence on the lowest-common-denominator solution, insufficient focus on end-users—threatened to attach themselves to IPng selection.

Yet the RFC observes that the three main proposals had few genuinely significant differences. The competitive process did not produce radical alternatives; rather, all three were incremental changes to proven technology. This could be viewed as either success (consensus, low risk) or failure (insufficient innovation). The value lay perhaps in the process itself, which might help repair the technical and social cohesion of the Internet Engineering community rather than in the selection of any particular proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: The three candidates were surprisingly similar. This could mean the process worked well (everyone agreed on the basics), or it could mean nobody was being bold enough. Either way, the process of choosing together probably mattered as much as which one won.
